title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
summary: Capacity estimation turns vague requirements into storage, QPS, bandwidth, and latency budgets. Good estimates are order-of-magnitude honest, explicit about assumptions, and revised when measurements arrive.

sections.title: Why estimate before drawing boxes
paragraphs: Estimates force requirements into numbers: daily active users, read/write ratio, object size, retention, peak-to-average. Without them, architectures are fashion.
Interview and production practice share the same skill: powers of ten, latency hierarchy, and stating assumptions out loud so others can challenge them.
An estimate that is 2× wrong is often useful; one that hides assumptions is dangerous.

sections.title: The latency and throughput vocabulary
paragraphs: Know approximate costs: L1/L2 cache nanoseconds, DRAM ~100ns, SSD tens to hundreds of µs, HDD ms, same-rack network ~100µs–1ms, cross-region 50–150ms+. These bound how many hops your p99 can afford.

QPS = concurrency / latency for a single server under saturation (Little's Law). If a handler averages 10ms and you want 10k QPS, you need ~100 concurrent in-flight requests — and enough CPU/IO to sustain them.
Bandwidth: 1 MB objects at 1000 writes/s is ~1 GB/s before replication and indexes. Replication factor and erasure coding multiply storage and sometimes network.

sections.title: Storage math
paragraphs: Rows × average size × indexes × retention × replication. Indexes often dominate. Compression helps sequential analytics more than point-lookup OLTP.
Time-series and logs: estimate ingest bytes/day and compaction overhead. 'Unlimited retention' is a cost decision, not a feature.

sections.title: Working the problem
paragraphs: Start from peak QPS and object size. Derive read QPS from write QPS × ratio. Check if a single shard fits; if not, partition. Check if cache can absorb reads given hit rate assumptions.
Always leave headroom (often 2–3×) for spikes, rebalancing, and incident recovery. Publish the assumptions next to the diagram.

deepDive.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Back-of-Envelope Estimation in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Back-of-Envelope Estimation include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Back-of-Envelope Estimation intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

practices: Use powers of ten; avoid false precision
Convert estimates into SLOs and capacity alerts
pitfalls: Ignoring indexes and replication in storage math
Designing for average instead of peak
Forgetting cross-region RTT in chatty APIs

examples.description: Online fanout vs inbox model driven by connection counts and QPS.

keyTakeaways: Estimates are decision tools, not predictions
Latency hierarchy constrains architecture more than brand names
whyItMatters: Every serious design review asks 'what scale?' Estimation is how you answer without hand-waving.
reflectionQuestions: What is the scarcest resource in your current service — CPU, RAM, disk, or network?
How would a 10× traffic spike change your diagram?
